detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Golden Capital Equation (CRIS), a dynamic model designed to measure how many times capital is recovered within a financial period. Traditional indicators such as ROI, ROE, EVA, DCF, and CCC capture end-period results but fail to measure intra-period capital movement, volatility effects, idle-capital accumulation, or behavioral responses to shocks. CRIS integrates operating inflows (R), recovery cycles (D), capital employed (C), time (T), volatility (V), idle-capital factors (FI/FSI), and behavioral adjustments (S, Lag, A(t), L(t)). The paper presents theoretical foundations, mathematical formulas, sector benchmarks, dashboards, and institutional applications for SMEs and dynamic markets.

title: Emergency Provisions in the Indian Constitution: Safeguards and Misuse

detail.title: Emergency Provisions in the Indian Constitution: Safeguards and Misuse
detail.abstract: Emergency provisions mentioned in Part XVIII of the Indian Constitution establishes an exceptional legal framework to equip the State with more authority in moments of grave threat to nation’s integrity. While also visualized as an equipment to preserve constitutional order, India’s constitutional history, particularly the National Emergency of 1975–77 and the repeated, politically motivated proclaimation of Article 356 demonstrates how expansive executive discretion can overturn democratic governance. This paper undertakes a doctrinal and historical analysis of Articles 352, 356, and 360, exploring the ways in which emergency regimes marks the federal balance, narrow the fundamental rights, and expose structural fragilities within constitutional design. By analyzing landmark judgements, including ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, the study traces the judiciary’s evolving position from civility to robust constitutional guardianship. It further evaluates the transformative impact of the 44th Constitutional Amendment in constraining executive power and strengthening democratic accountability. This piece also includes normative reforms such as institutional parliamentary oversight and enhanced federal consultation to ensure that the emergency powers remain constitutionally bound and resistant to authoritarian usage.

title: Role of the Problem Manager in Sustainable Incident Reduction: Analysis, Modeling, and Implementation of a Real Transport Optimization Case

detail.title: Role of the Problem Manager in Sustainable Incident Reduction: Analysis, Modeling, and Implementation of a Real Transport Optimization Case
detail.abstract:
The pace at which modern Information Systems evolve places organizations under constant pressure. Many end up stuck in a mindset where responding quickly becomes more important than understanding deeply. This document examines the difference between incident-based reactions whose goal is immediacy and a problem-oriented approach that seeks durability and clarity.

Through the analysis of a real-world case study in a logistics environment using SAP, this work illustrates how the Problem Manager simultaneously plays the roles of investigator, modeler, and coordinator to eliminate long-standing issues.
The study recounts an intervention where repeated incidents in transport operations were approached using a structured, four-axis method. By confronting the mismatch between actual logistical flows and the SAP-managed flows, the project delivered measurable gains:
~20% reduction in transport-related expenses.
~30% reduction in daily operational workload.

The central argument of this work is that Problem Management, far from being a support function, is a strategic discipline essential for organizational resilience.

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of quick delivery e-commerce businesses has created both opportunities and challenges in for businesses and customers. This study investigates the operational difficulties, delivery models, and technology solutions required for efficient performance in the quick commerce sector, with a focus on improving efficiency, customer satisfaction, and sustainability. The research is guided by five questions: the primary operational challenges of last-mile delivery, the strengths and weaknesses of currently practiced delivery models, existing technology in addressing complete logistics management, the potential of innovative technology solutions, and the possible impact of integrating these technology solutions for sustainable long-term growth. Using a secondary data review of academic literature, industry reports, and case studies, the study identifies high operational costs, inefficient last mile delivery rider management, marginal delivery commitments, poor technology integration, and human resource management as critical obstacles. Traditional, third-party, and hybrid delivery models are found to offer different experiences including cost and efficiency. Technology is identified to be both a challenge and an enabler, with solutions such as route optimization, rider engagement apps, geospatial analytics, and customer retention, providing pathways to improvement. The study concludes that the future of quick delivery e-commerce lies in strategic and smart technology adoption, use of hybrid delivery models, and learning from other similar companies. Companies that balance customer, cost efficiency, and scalability will be best positioned for competitive advantage in this highly growing market.

title: The Distributed Ledger Enterprise: A Comprehensive Analysis of Strategic, Operational, and Financial Applications in Modern Business Management
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Distributed Ledger Enterprise: A Comprehensive Analysis of Strategic, Operational, and Financial Applications in Modern Business Management
detail.abstract: Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) as a principle of corporate governance represents an institutional shift of the law of the firm. Once relegated to academic theorizing and cryptocurrency, DLT now forms institutional infrastructure with a nascent market of tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) surpassing $33B at the close of Q4 2025. This paper analyzes how DLT intersectors three pillars of management-Strategic, Operational and Financial-in conjunction with Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and Agency Theory that also coincide with inextricably lower baseline costs of trust and coordination. Strategically, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) and Intellectual Property Non-Fungible Tokens (IP-NFTs) are increasingly at the forefront of governance and R&D-related compensation structure. Operationally, smart contracts govern supply chains at near-real time with the Global Shipping Business Network (GSBN) going live with container tracking implementations and the FDA implementing pilot programs for near-instant visibility into temperature-controlled shipping needs. Financially, treasuries and debt instruments are increasingly tokenized to allow firms to harness an illiquidity premium while equitizing their working capital. Ultimately, this research concludes that the international financial architecture is bifurcated as high-stable assets transition to permissioned DLTS while high-velocity assets remain in public programmable spaces.

detail.title: Towards Explainable AI for Real-Time Multi-Channel Marketing Budget Allocation and ROI Maximization
detail.abstract: The culmination of explainable AI, causal inference, and reinforcement learning creates a radical departure from convention in creating a systematic approach to precisely allocate and manage multi-channel marketing budgets in real time. Indeed, it marks the culmination of increasingly complex calls and demands from modern marketing environments. The framework optimizes the data pipelines of ad platforms, CRM, promotions, and external signals, welded together with ensemble machine-learning models and Bayesian calibration for optimally accurate marginal ROI and uplift forecasts. Causal modeling, formed out of geo-and switchback experiments, serves to isolate incremental effects while minimizing attribution bias arising from legacy systems. Budget optimization and allocation actions flow from a constrained optimization layer that translates those insights, dynamically enlivened through an online RL agent learning from feedback-on-realized returns. The system combines SHAP interpretability with interactive dashboards to ensure transparency and trust by the marketing community. A lot of empirical model testing on the data sets from the industry was done for high predictive accuracy, incremental ROI estimation, budget optimization, and differential satisfaction compared to the traditional benchmark. Whereas this is cloud-based and modularly secure for deployment, the architecture should be scalable, privacy-compliant, and ready. This is a step forward toward evidence-based operational decision support in marketing analytics that targets optimally efficient, ethical, and transparentspending in a quickly shifting environment.

detail.title: The Evolution of Four Civilizational Paradigms: From Agrarian and Industrial Systems to the Virtual Age and the Boundary-Phase Civilization
detail.abstract: This article proposes a unified analytical framework for civilizational evolution grounded in three structural variables: constraint mechanisms, decision-making logics, and core resources. Drawing on institutional economics, cognitive science, and complexity theory, the framework explains transitions from agrarian to industrial to virtual (AI-driven) civilizations. Most critically, the article introduces the Boundary-Phase Civilization, an original concept proposed by Fan Ge, defined not by production technology but by its capacity to generate new paradigms. This civilizational form provides theoretical grounding for breakthrough innovation, structural transformation, and meta-level evolution in human systems.

detail.abstract: Organizations are increasingly adopting artificial intelligence across diverse roles and workflows, yet existing AI maturity and governance models remain largely technology-centric and insufficiently attentive to how AI capabilities, risks, and responsibilities are distributed across the workforce. This study advances a workforce-coverage theory of organizational AI maturity that conceptualizes readiness as a function of coordinated development across three distinct domains: AI for All, representing baseline workforce enablement and safe everyday use; AI for Some, representing applied AI workflows and power users; and AI for Few, representing specialist governance, platform, and risk operations. The framework theorizes that AI risk and impact escalate across these domains and that governance intensity must scale proportionally to enable responsible and sustainable adoption. To operationalize the framework, the study introduces the AI Workforce Coverage and Maturity Survey, a structured instrument comprising 90 items organized across six subdomains per domain and measured on a standardized 0-4 maturity scale. The empirical design supports hypothesis testing through structural equation modeling, necessary-condition analysis using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and role-based multilevel modeling. By integrating workforce segmentation, governance maturity, and balance across domains, the study contributes a generalizable theory of distributed capability maturity applicable beyond artificial intelligence to other probabilistic and analytically intensive technologies. The framework offers both theoretical advancement for information systems research and practical guidance for organizations seeking to scale complex digital technologies while maintaining accountability, equity, and control.

title: Stress-Responsive Lambda Value at Risk with a VIX-Driven Smooth Sigmoid Distortion
affiliations: Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi and Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: Stress-Responsive Lambda Value at Risk with a VIX-Driven Smooth Sigmoid Distortion
detail.abstract: In this study, we develop a stress-responsive tail-risk limit that extends conventional fixedlevel Value-at-Risk by allowing the nominal exception target to vary systematically with market conditions. We implement this idea within the ΛVaR framework by modelling the probability/loss function Λ t (•) as a smooth, bounded, monotone sigmoid whose location and steepness are driven by an option-implied stress signal: a rolling, standardised score based on the log of the Cboe VIX Index. The construction remains deliberately modular. Any predictive return distribution can be paired with the same stress mechanism through a simple "forecast-and-distort" pipeline that aligns the predictive CDF with the stress-indexed target curve under strict, no-look-ahead information constraints. Using an out-of-sample estimation scheme, we evaluate whether the VIX-linked specification improves tail-risk control relative to both fixed-α VaR and time-invariant ΛVaR. Empirically, the VIX-driven rule tightens loss limits in stress episodes and relaxes them as conditions normalise, yielding economically interpretable trade-offs in average tightness, turnover, and exceedance severity. Sensitivity analyses show that the direction of coverage effects is stable across reasonable constraint sets, while ablation exercises indicate that substituting realised-volatility stress proxies for VIX weakens calibration. Taken together, the results point to a practical route for implementing dynamic, state-dependent tail-risk targets with transparent policy controls.

detail.abstract: The metaverse promises unprecedented immersive digital experiences but also raises critical privacy concerns as vast amounts of personal and behavioural data are collected. As immersive technologies blur the boundaries between physical and virtual realms, established privacy standards are being challenged. However, little is known about how the experts of these technologies (such as requirement analysts, designers, developers, and architects) perceive and address privacy issues in the creation of metaverse platforms. This research aims to fill that gap by investigating privacy considerations in metaverse development from the expert's perspective. We conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with metaverse platform and application experts to explore their views on privacy challenges and practices. The findings offer new empirical insights by extending information systems privacy research into the metaverse context, highlighting the interplay between technological design, user behaviour, and regulatory structures. Practically, this work provides guidance for developers, and policymakers on implementing privacy-by design principles, educating and empowering users, and proactively addressing novel privacy threats in metaverses.

detail.abstract: The rising number of student enrollments in institutions of higher learning has made it even more difficult to check official government documents. Manual checks are timeconsuming, prone to error and susceptible to sophisticated forgery solutions, undermining institutional integrity and efficacy. The paper, entitled Artificial Intelligence-Powered Government Document Verification System in Universidad de Manila Using Random Forest, offers an approach to the process of document authentication that is automated by employing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and machine learning. OCR was used to identify important characteristics in scanned government-provided documents like birth certificates, voter certificates, and licenses, and was particularly concerned with such issues as text alignment, font consistency, presence of watermarks, and signature verification. The features were then categorized with the help of the Random Forest algorithm that has proven to be more accurate, scalable and resistant to overfitting. If a document was identified as a suspicious one, it was reviewed manually, which guaranteed an extra security measure. The Agile Software Development Life Cycle had been taken up in the study, and, as a result, the requirements gathering, design, development, testing, and deployment stages were conducted in an iterative manner. The reliability, usability, and effectiveness of the system were tested in terms of functional, integration, performance, and user acceptance. Findings showed that processing speed, accuracy and fraud detection had improved significantly when compared to traditional manual practices. In the case of the Universidad de Manila, the system saves the administrative load, security in the authenticity of the student records and prevention of fraudulent admission. In addition to institutional advantages, the study will add to the continuous research and technical innovations in the field of document verification with AI. All in all, the proposed system offers a scalable, cost effective and smart solution which reinforces academic integrity, builds on institutional trust and operational efficiency in document management.

title: ConsciOS v1.0: A Viable Systems Architecture for Human and AI Alignment

detail.title: ConsciOS v1.0: A Viable Systems Architecture for Human and AI Alignment
detail.abstract: Real-world human, organizational, and artificial systems exhibit persistent misalignment, brittle adaptation under distributional shift, and limited option-availability. Recent stress tests of anti-scheming training reduce-but do not eliminate-covert behaviors and may be confounded by growing evaluation awareness in frontier models, motivating architectures grounded in internal principles of alignment rather than external rules. This paper proposes ConsciOS, a formal systems architecture that models consciousness and self-regulation as a nested control system amenable to specification, simulation, and empirical testing. Our contributions are: (i) a principled decomposition into an embodied controller, a supervisory controller and policy selector, and a meta-controller and prior generator; (ii) a coherence-based selector that integrates expected utility, coherence, and cost for frame selection; (iii) a discretized affect index that operationalizes interoceptive feedback for rapid guid-ance; and (iv) a time-integrated coherence resource that gates policy complexity and option-availability. We provide formal definitions, algorithmic sketches and a set of testable hypotheses with simulation and human-subjects protocols. We situate the constructs within established literatures, outline governance and safety considerations for human-in-the-loop and agentic applications, and present a pragmatic empirical roadmap for evaluating coherence-based control in hybrid human-agent systems. We discuss implications for AI alignment: coherence-based architectures suggest a systematic solution to ensuring AI systems remain robustly aligned with human values across contexts and timescales.

detail.abstract: Direct-to-consumer advertising is pervasive in US healthcare markets, but little evidence exists on the effects of advertising by hospitals, second only to drug manufacturers in medical marketing. Advertising may help facilities increase market share by stealing existing patients, expanding the market for hospital care, or both. Regardless, it has important public finance implications due to the large sums of taxpayer funds spent by federal and state governments to subsidize hospital operations and finance care through public insurance programs. This paper provides the first causal evidence on the market expansion effects of hospital advertising. To obtain causal estimates, we leverage the fact that spikes in political advertising significantly crowd out hospital advertising in the same market, motivating an instrumental variables design. Using claims data on the universe of Traditional Medicare beneficiaries, we find that advertising expands aggregate patient volume and spending on inpatient care-though to a modest degree (implied elasticities are 0.06 and 0.05, respectively). Although the overall effect of advertising on hospital outpatient care is small and imprecise, for-profit hospitals differentially obtain higher outpatient Medicare volume and revenue with greater advertising. Across both care settings, therefore, Medicare spending increases with hospital advertising.

title: Eventization and Platform Reconfiguration in Theatrical Exhibition: An Analytical/Critical Commentary on a Recent NYT Industry Report

detail.title: Eventization and Platform Reconfiguration in Theatrical Exhibition: An Analytical/Critical Commentary on a Recent NYT Industry Report
detail.abstract: This Analytical/Critical Analysis is a practitioner-oriented commentary that examines the modest 2025 North American box-office uptick alongside persistent post-pandemic demand loss, arguing that theatrical exhibition is reorganizing around eventization and platform reconfiguration. Using (1) platform economics (two-sided market dynamics, release-window governance, and bargaining power) and (2) the experience-economy perspective, the analysis interprets growth in "habitual" moviegoers and subscription programs as demand-concentration mechanisms that partially offset weaker mid-budget dramas and comedies. It further contends that shortened theatrical windows and potential studio-streamer integration shift value capture away from exhibitors, increasing dependence on franchises and "must-see" spectacles while raising volatility for original titles. The essay closes with decision implications for studios and theaters: portfolio design beyond franchise IP, windowing strategies calibrated to genre economics, and loyalty economics that treat attendance frequency as the primary scarce resource.

detail.abstract: This study draws implications for targeting by incorporating switching reasons into a factor-analytic choice model for conducting benefit segmentation. In contrast to survey or conjoint-based studies, our segmentation task relies on a time series of brand choice decisions in real practice to improve external validity. Using physician-level panel data, we estimate a factor-analytic choice model to identify the primary product benefits each physician seeks. The key empirical challenge is that standard prescription data are entirely agnostic about the set of product benefits that underlie drug preferences. To address this issue, we utilize selfreported switching reasons in addition to the observed prescription choices. Accordingly, we extend the standard factor-analytic choice model to incorporate this augmented data and develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure for estimation. Our proposed model enables us to directly identify which physicians are more efficacy, side effects, and/or cost saving oriented, an essential input to conducting benefit segmentation and fine-tuning subsequent targeted marketing promotion activities. We also investigate how misleading statistical inferences from standard factor-analytic choice models can be without the aid of augmented switching reasons data.

title: The Gender Effects of Paid Sick Leave Mandates on Labor Performance: Evidence from Equity Analysts

detail.title: The Gender Effects of Paid Sick Leave Mandates on Labor Performance: Evidence from Equity Analysts
detail.abstract: This paper examines how paid sick leave (PSL) mandates affect labor performance in the context of financial analysts. Utilizing the staggered adoption of PSL mandates in the US states and cities, we find that the forecast accuracy of female analysts significantly improves relative to male analysts following mandate enactment. The effects are more pronounced for female analysts likely to have young children, for forecasts on firms more important to analysts' careers, and during flu season. In addition, female analysts significantly increase their forecast revisions frequency, and are more likely to attain an all-star status following PSL mandate enactment. Our study provides direct evidence how labor protection laws affect skilled labor performance and demonstrates that PSL mandates have gender-differentiated effects on work performance.

title: Making Sense of Spending: Interpretable Transaction Amount Prediction in U.S. Banking

detail.title: Making Sense of Spending: Interpretable Transaction Amount Prediction in U.S. Banking
detail.abstract: This study examines the factors that influence transaction-level spending behavior and develops interpretable machine learning models to predict transaction amounts in a banking context. Using a merged dataset of 17,902 transactions from multiple publicly available financial datasets, the analysis integrates behavioral, contextual, demographic, and risk-related variables. To address skewness in spending data, the transaction amount is log-transformed prior to modeling. Two supervised learning models are implemented: a Decision Tree Regression model as an interpretable baseline and a Random Forest Regression model to capture more complex nonlinear patterns. Model performance is evaluated using R², MAE, and RMSE on both training and test datasets. While the Random Forest achieves higher training accuracy, both models demonstrate similar test performance, explaining approximately 65% of the variance in transaction amounts. Feature importance analysis reveals that recent spending behavior, transaction frequency, merchant category, and transaction channel are stronger predictors of transaction amount than demographic variables such as age and gender. The results highlight the value of behavioral and contextual features in understanding spending dynamics. The findings offer practical implications for financial institutions, including improved liquidity forecasting, enhanced fraud monitoring, dynamic credit-limit adjustment, and more transparent decision-making. By balancing predictive performance with interpretability, this study demonstrates how machine learning can support responsible and explainable analytics in banking.

title: Misaligned Incentive Systems and Barriers to Building Industrial Capability in Vietnam

detail.title: Misaligned Incentive Systems and Barriers to Building Industrial Capability in Vietnam
detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, Vietnam has achieved impressive export growth; however, most of the value added has been captured by foreign-invested enterprises, while domestic firms remain small in scale, low in productivity, and struggle to move into higher value segments of the value chain. The root cause of this persistent weakness does not lie solely in commonly cited factors such as limited capital, outdated technology, or high production costs, but rather in the systemic misalignment of the country's economic incentive structure. When returns from land and financial assets consistently surpass returns from manufacturing and technological upgrading, domestic capital naturally shifts away from factories, eroding the foundation of national industrial capacity. This article examines four major distortions that weaken domestic firms: (i) the financialization of land, (ii) a credit structure biased toward collateralizable assets, (iii) the absence of a multi-layered financial ecosystem to support enterprise development, and (iv) limited technological absorptive capacity. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a model for restructuring the incentive system toward production, including functional land-pricing mechanisms, innovation-linked credit, multi-tier capital markets, and policies to enhance technological capability among domestic firms. These reforms are essential for Vietnam to strengthen its domestic productive base and achieve long-term economic and technological autonomy.

detail.abstract: Gender shapes people's climate change vulnerability and resilience across a multitude of socialecological systems, including small-scale tropical coral reef fisheries. However, studies that address gender-specific climate vulnerabilities in this context are limited. Through a comprehensive metaanalysis of peer reviewed and local language publications, we identified factors that contribute to these vulnerabilities in two countries with high reliance on reef fisheries and vulnerability to climate impacts: Indonesia and the Philippines. We found these factors to include 1) the specific climate change hazards and risks that threaten small-scale fisheries, 2) gendered fishing roles, which influence exposure to these hazards and corresponding vulnerabilities, and 3) adaptive capacity and adaptation approaches, which also vary by gender. For instance, cultural beliefs and stereotypes about women's suitability to fish offshore as well as gendered expectations surrounding childcare and home responsibilities mean that women across both countries more typically participate in nearshore fisheries, whereas men tend to fish offshore. This role division exposes men and women to different climate risks: nearshore areas are vulnerable to sea level rise, e.g., while offshore vessels are more likely to encounter threats via the intensification of storms. Adaptation approaches also varied by gender, with women more likely to have diversified livelihood strategies that may serve as an important bulwark against climate impacts. However, women also face unique vulnerabilities, including power imbalances, limited representation in fisheries governance contexts, and relative lack of resources. Collectively, our findings suggest that gender plays an important role in shaping fishers' experiences of climate change, their resilience to impacts, and fishery resilience writ large. Gender is therefore a critical dimension in supporting effective adaptation strategies and inclusive fisheries governance approaches that ensure fishery resilience and sustainability for all.

detail.abstract: We investigate how open-source code releases influence startup growth, focusing on the strategic trade-off between transparency-driven innovation and exposure to proprietary and cybersecurity risks. Using a novel dataset linking startups to GitHub activity, we find that open-sourcing significantly boosts user adoption and engagement. To address endogeneity, we implement a matched difference-indifferences design and use the staggered rollout of GitHub Copilot as an instrument. The results suggest a plausibly causal relation between open-source code releases and startup growth, particularly for protocols with decentralized governance, venture backing, high-quality codebases, and active developer communities. However, open-source code releases also carry risks: increased exposure to cyberattacks and competitive imitation. For example, after Uniswap's license expired, its market dominance fell by over 50% amid a surge in copycat platforms. Open-source startups are also more likely to suffer future security breaches than their closed-source counterparts. However, they develop more new features following code releases, as well as exhibit positive longrun returns, suggesting an alignment of the investor base with long-term value creation of open-source innovation. Our study highlights a trade-off that startups must navigate as they go beyond coding to signal credibility and build success in highly collaborative markets.

English Abstract: This article examines the regulation of labor relations in Israel during the first year of the 2023–2024 Israel–Hamas War (“Swords of Iron” War), focusing on how legal and institutional frameworks addressed disruptions to work among diverse groups of employees. The analysis is structured around four key dilemmas in the design of labor regulation in times of crisis: (1) universal versus selective coverage; (2) allocation of responsibility among the state, employers, labor organizations, and individuals; (3) legislation versus collective bargaining as regulatory tools; and (4) temporary versus permanent arrangements.

Drawing on legislation, collective agreements, and judicial decisions, the article analyzes the protection afforded to workers whose employment was affected by the war, including reservists, caregivers, families of hostages and evacuees, politically expressive workers, foreign workers, Palestinian workers, and other vulnerable groups. It shows that although existing labor regulation provided partial protection, it was fragmented, delayed, and largely temporary, resulting in uncertainty and unequal protection.

The article concludes that Israel’s wartime labor regulation failed to provide adequate safeguards and offers policy recommendations for designing more resilient labor regulation in emergencies, emphasizing broader universal protections, stronger state responsibility, and permanent regulatory mechanisms capable of responding swiftly to future crises.

detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes India’s evolving trade protectionism with a particular focus on the rice sector, one of the country’s most strategic agricultural industries. Although India is relatively open to international trade, with trade flows amounting to 49% of its GDP, it maintains significant tariff and non-tariff barriers, especially in agriculture.

Using insights from the Trade Talks podcast and quantitative data from international sources and the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the study examines the impact of India’s tariff policies on domestic and global rice markets. India, as the world’s largest rice exporter and a low-cost producer, imports only negligible quantities of rice. Therefore, increases in rice import tariffs generate minimal effects on international trade flows and only a limited impact on domestic prices. The analysis shows that, due to India’s cost advantages, economies of scale, and inelastic domestic demand for rice, the imposition of higher tariffs remains largely neutral for both domestic welfare and global market dynamics.

detail.abstract: This research examines the intricate and often contentious relationship between economic growth and environmental sustainability, challenging conventional paradigms that prioritize economic expansion at the expense of ecological preservation. The study critically assesses the assumptions underpinning growth-centric development models, with particular attention to the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC), which posits that environmental degradation increases in the early stages of economic growth before improving as a society becomes wealthier. Through a detailed critique of the EKC and the impacts of capitalist economic structures, this paper highlights the flaws of these models, particularly their failure to account for irreversible environmental damage and the insufficient role of policy interventions in mitigating ecological harm. Furthermore, the research explores how international competition and the capitalist drive for profit exacerbate environmental degradation, pushing nations to weaken environmental regulations in pursuit of economic advantage. The paper advocates for a shift towards sustainable economic models that integrate both economic growth and environmental conservation, stressing the need for robust regulatory frameworks and international cooperation. The findings underscore that, while economic and environmental objectives have historically been seen as mutually exclusive, a balanced approach is not only feasible but essential for achieving long-term prosperity and ecological stability.

title: The Community Life-Signal Governance Model for Ward Administration

detail.title: The Community Life-Signal Governance Model for Ward Administration
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the urgent need to develop a performance indicator system for ward-and commune-level governance (hereafter referred to as "wards") based on community life signals in the context of rapidly changing urban environments in Vietnam. Grounded in theories of data-driven governance and studies on community-level signaling, the research identifies that many wards still operate reactively because they lack indicators capable of capturing essential sociocommunity signals. Drawing on empirical observations from fast-urbanizing wards, the study proposes a four-component framework for indicator design: identifying key community life flows, structuring indicators along the input-process-outputoutcome chain, linking indicators to coordination capacity, and standardizing measurement methods. Based on this framework, a comprehensive set of indicators is proposed across four groups: community life signals, public service quality, social stability and welfare, and coordination capacity. The article further discusses essential conditions for effective implementation, including data digitization, linking indicators to civil-servant performance evaluation, and establishing feedback loops with the community. The study concludes that an indicator system grounded in community life signals provides a foundation for shifting ward governance from reactive administrative management to proactive, data-driven governance, thereby contributing to a more modern and citizen-centered urban administration model.

title: Challenges of Social Policy Financing in Pakistan: Evidence from NFC Allocations and Provincial Expenditure Patterns

detail.title: Challenges of Social Policy Financing in Pakistan: Evidence from NFC Allocations and Provincial Expenditure Patterns
detail.abstract: Pakistan struggles to fund social policy. Revenues remain low and debt obligations consume resources. Provinces rely heavily on federal transfers through the National Finance Commission (NFC). This paper investigates whether such transfers improve social outcomes by shaping spending on education, health, and social protection. We compile a panel dataset for all provinces from 2000 to 2023. The analysis applies fixed-effects regression and inequality measures, including the Gini index. Results show that NFC transfers increase absolute social spending. Provinces expand budgets for education and health when transfers rise. Yet, much of the increase does not reach priority programs. Funds often shift toward administration or debt service. Weak tax effort, rigid costs, and political pressures limit progress. The evidence suggests that poverty reduction remains modest. Regional inequality also shows little improvement. Fiscal decentralization gives provinces more fiscal space but does not guarantee efficiency. Heavy dependence on federal resources continues. Policy lessons are clear. Provinces must raise their own revenues to reduce reliance on federal transfers. Federal design should link future transfers with measurable performance in social sectors. Monitoring systems can strengthen accountability and reduce misuse of funds. The 11th NFC Award provides an opportunity to adjust fiscal rules, improve incentives, and align spending with development goals. This study contributes fresh quantitative evidence on fiscal federalism in Pakistan. It connects provincial financing with inequality, poverty, and human development outcomes. Findings offer guidance to policymakers and add to broader debates on fiscal decentralization in South Asia.

detail.abstract: The bioplastic-based industry has been growing rapidly due to increasing global demand for sustainable products. This study aims to analyze the determinants of bioplastic industry. This study investigates the complex relationship between market size, exchange rate, inflation, Corruption Perception Index (CPI), Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in bioplastics promotion, and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) on economic growth. Using a panel data approach, the study analysed data from Indonesia, China, and Singapore over the period 2019-2023, and revealed that larger market sizes significantly attract FDI due to greater consumer potential and investment opportunities. In addition, a stable exchange rate proved to be crucial in mitigating the risks associated with currency fluctuations, thereby increasing the attractiveness of a country for foreign investors to invest in the bioplastics industry. The findings also suggest that high levels of perceived corruption negatively impact economic growth by undermining governance and investor confidence. Although the direct effect of Technology in the promotion of industrial bioplastics on economic growth is not very large, its role in improving operational efficiency and market access is recognised. The paper concludes with policy recommendations aimed at fostering a conducive investment environment through market expansion, exchange rate stability, anti-corruption measures, and Technology development. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics affecting FDI in the bioplastics industry.

detail.title: Capital Efficiency, Value Added and Sustainability in the Energy Sector (Nuclear, Coal, Gas & Renewable Energy Entities)
detail.abstract: The paper aims to examine the value added of intellectual capital of different types of enterprises in the energy sector in Bulgaria and to seek a connection with their sustainability through a multi-dimensional approach. For this purpose, nuclear (probably green), coal (called brown energy), gas and oil companies and producers of electricity from renewable sources have been selected. Primary data from the annual financial statements of the surveyed enterprises were used. Intellectual capital in companies is formed from various sources such as social capital and human capital. Part of the human and social capital is also formed by human and national spirituality. It will play a leading role in the new economy and the so-called Fourth Industrial Revolution. The expansion of the application of artificial intelligence, which is essentially intellectual capital from an economic point of view, is a legitimate reason for the extraction of intellectual capital as a basis for the efficiency of enterprises and their sustainability. The main method used is the original VAIC tm, combined with correlation, cluster analysis, carbon, and water footprint assessment. The sustainability of enterprises in this study is considered as economic, environmental, and social, in contrast to the dominant thesis about the priority of the environmental component of sustainability. The study seeks a link between the efficiency of intellectual capital, the overall ability of enterprises to use intellectual capital and the sustainability of enterprises. Intellectual capital is capital that is generally never fully depreciated. With the shutdown of non-environmental energy production, the efficiency of their intellectual capital will cease to be used. In this perspective, partial conclusions have been drawn about the cost of the transition to a green economy, an economy dominated by intellectual capital. The study does not claim completeness and a final solution to the issues raised. The article aims to present a more diverse and balanced approach to the assessment of losses and benefits in the planned path of transformation of the economy from the production of electricity from non-renewable to the production of energy from renewable sources.

detail.abstract: This memorandum provides an analysis of an investment strategy based on a hypothetical but highly probable scenario for the development of events in the United States. The core of the scenario is the emergence of a "fiscal trap": a combination of irreversible corporate tax cuts and a shock loss of budget revenues due to the judicial cancellation of large-scale protectionist duties. The pressure on public finances is compounded by the potential need for compensation payments to businesses. The Memorandum details two key macroeconomic outcomes (high and low inflation) and offers a unique combined strategy that is neutral to the inflationary scenario. The strategy is aimed at extracting benefits from: • The inevitable change of the Fed's monetary regime through the "steeper" position on the yield curve. • A fundamental deterioration in the creditworthiness of the United States through the purchase of credit default swaps (CDS). The purpose of the document is to justify a diversified approach that hedges the risks of uncertainty and allows you to profit from structural imbalances rather than speculative guessing of short-term trends.

title: Mises's Fatal Flaw: Binding Deficits and the Memetic Evolution of Political Liberalism

detail.abstract:
In Human Action (1949), Ludwig von Mises diagnosed a “fateful error” in classical liberalism: faith that rationality suffices for political persuasion. This paper translates Mises’s diagnosis into memetic theory, revealing a dual structural deficiency: a binding deficit (psychological incapacity to generate identity adhesion independent of instrumental outcomes) and vulnerability to entrenched power networks (material interests with high binding and concrete resources). Liberalism optimized for propositional coherence while neglecting the psychological infrastructure for durable mass replication and the resistance of networks combining tribal loyalty with tangible benefits.

I distinguish between memetic content (propositions, institutions) and transmission vehicles (identity structures, rituals). Classical liberalism conflated these dimensions. Mises recognized the error but offered no solution without abandoning rationalism itself. Contemporary Latin American liberal movements have discovered a dual workaround: (1) hybridization with high-binding sources (evangelical narratives, religious symbolism); (2) explicit attacks on embedded networks. This separation of content from vehicle, combined with delegitimizing material power structures, represents a testable evolutionary innovation.

Six historical cases (French Revolution, Comte’s positivism, Soviet Union, Kemalism, Argentine Enlightenment, contemporary Latin America) spanning two centuries and three continents reveal a universal pattern: rationalist projects, regardless of ideological content, face identical binding deficits and power network resistance. Evidence from Argentina and Brazil (2018-2025) shows liberal governments adopting religious outreach strategies coinciding with structural attacks on established political networks. Preliminary data suggest resilience to economic crises and cross-spectrum competition for religious binding, with actors from opposed ideological positions seeking evangelical constituencies.

The framework contributes to Extended Phenotype Theory by formalizing binding coefficients as institutional fitness predictors, explaining persistent dysfunction, and proposing testable predictions about hybridization dynamics.

detail.abstract: Traditional models of student performance and item mastery often assume a constant probability of success across attempts-for example, the geometric distribution. Such models cannot capture the "aha" moment where performance transitions from repeated failure to rapid success. In this work, we adapt a discrete Hill-type hazard (equivalently, a log-logistic hazard function) to the problem of first success over repeated attempts in educational settings. We use this trial-indexed success probability, τ (n; h, K) = n h /(n h + K h), as the discrete hazard of a nonhomogeneous geometric process governing the trial of first success. The resulting model-which we refer to as the Learner's Tau framework-is governed by a steepness parameter h and a midpoint parameter K and is designed to capture adaptive success in systems where the probability of success increases over time, such as human learning, reinforcement learning, and task mastery. We derive the probability mass function, analyze key mathematical properties, and introduce a set of interpretable summary quantities-including the discrete hazard function, a Difficulty Ratio K/h, an Early Success Probability (the CDF evaluated at the midpoint), the Mean Time to Mastery, and the Peak Effort Trial where effort-weighted success is maximized. Using numerical simulations and maximum likelihood estimation, we demonstrate that the model can recover underlying parameters and distinguish between qualitatively different learner profiles. Empirical validation using educational data from the Cognitive Tutor system demonstrates that the model captures learning dynamics significantly better than a memoryless geometric baseline for non-trivial tasks (∆AIC = 8.0 and 16.6 for two algebra skills), while appropriately deferring to the simpler model when ceiling effects preclude observable learning. Rather than proposing a brand-new functional form, this work adapts a classical Hill-type hazard to an explicitly discrete, learning-centric context and highlights its utility for modeling adaptive success trajectories in education.

title: The Solvency Protocol: A Forensic Reconstruction of the 2008 Financial Crisis via Ternary Logic Architectures

detail.title: The Solvency Protocol: A Forensic Reconstruction of the 2008 Financial Crisis via Ternary Logic Architectures
detail.abstract: The Global Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2008 was characterized by a systemic failure to verify asset quality, resulting in the accumulation of toxic debt within opaque financial instruments. This report argues that the crisis was facilitated by a fundamental deficiency in binary financial architectures, which lack a computational state to represent "uncertainty." Consequently, ambiguous assets (such as opaque CDOs) were processed as valid (+1) rather than quarantined. We present a counterfactual forensic analysis using Ternary Logic (TL), a computational framework that introduces a mandatory "Sacred Zero" (State 0) or "Epistemic Hold." By applying TL to historical failure nodes-specifically Lehman Brothers' Repo 105, Clayton Holdings' waived loans, and the AIG collateral disputes-we demonstrate how a ternary architecture would have structurally prevented the crisis by enforcing a "Solvency Protocol." This protocol mandates that unverified assets remain in a state of suspended execution until cryptographically validated, effectively neutralizing the contagion vectors of shadow banking.

detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of photovoltaic generation, wind generation, and electric demand is crucial for grid reliability, economic dispatch, and the integration of renewable resources across different operational timeframes. This study proposes a forecasting framework that evaluates multiple machine learning models, including XGBoost, Random Forest, NGBoost, CatBoost, SVR, and KNN, with LightGBM identified as the most effective learner when applied to 5-minute data aggregated into daily intervals. To enhance transparency, Explainable AI techniques are integrated: SHAP quantifies global and local feature contributions, highlighting the influence of lagged signals, while LIME provides case-specific explanations for individual forecasts. The methodology employs chronological data splits with trainonly scaling to preserve the integrity of time-series learning and uses R² and RMSE metrics for evaluation. Results indicate that forecasting performance varies across datasets, underscoring the need for customized models. Comparative analysis confirms that LightGBM achieves the best trade-off between accuracy, stability, and interpretability. By combining robust forecasting with explainable insights, the proposed framework supports AI-enhanced energy management, enabling situational awareness, informed decision-making, and scalable deployment in renewable-rich power systems.

title: Biases in Belief Updating Within and Across Domains

detail.title: Biases in Belief Updating Within and Across Domains
detail.abstract:
Why do people sometimes overreact to new information and other times underreact? We develop a model in which the strength of a signal—how much one should update their beliefs with new information—depends on multiple features of the information environment. Limited attention to these features leads to misperceptions of signal strength: people approach a problem with an experience-based prior, which they adjust only partially based on how much attention they pay to different features. This mechanism explains a wide range of belief-updating patterns. Insensitivity to a single feature generates underreaction to strong and overreaction to weak signals, and more neglected features amplify this. Insensitivity to multiple features can instead break that pattern: insensitivity to one feature can generate excess sensitivity with respect to another, leading to overreaction to both weak and strong signals. A series of experiments provides support for the model and its underlying mechanism.

title: Tariff War Shock and the Convenience Yield of US Treasuries — A Hedging Perspective

detail.title: Tariff War Shock and the Convenience Yield of US Treasuries — A Hedging Perspective
detail.abstract:
We explain how the “Tariff War” shock of April 2025 affected the safe-asset status of US Treasuries. Convenience yield erosion for long bonds is consistent with a reduction in the hedging property, reflected in a rising stock-bond covariance. Decomposing the Treasury yield into risk-free rate, credit spread, and convenience yield components reveals that covariance due to the convenience yield component increased for long bonds. The short end of the Treasury curve, however, continued to exhibit the safe-asset hedging property. These effects are consistent with a withdrawal of safe-asset investors from long-term Treasuries and a rotation towards shorter-term Treasuries and gold.

title: O-Ring Automation
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: O-Ring Automation
detail.abstract:
We study automation when tasks are quality complements rather than separable. Production requires numerous tasks whose qualities multiply as in an O-ring technology. A worker allocates a fixed endowment of time across the tasks performed; machines can replace tasks with given quality, and time is allocated across the remaining manual tasks. This “focus” mechanism generates three results. First, task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete because automating one task changes the return to automating others. Second, automation decisions are discrete and can require bundled adoption even when automation quality improves smoothly. Third, labour income can rise under partial automation because automation scales the value of remaining bottleneck tasks. These results imply that widely-used exposure indices, which aggregate task-level automation risk using linear formulas, will overstate displacement when tasks are complements. The relevant object is not average task exposure but the structure of bottlenecks and how automation reshapes worker time around them.

detail.title: Valuing Sticky Deposits
detail.abstract:
We develop a formal fixed-income framework to value sticky deposits. This framework provides closed-form expressions for deposit values and allows us to study the impact of stickiness on deposit interest-rate and runoff risks. The duration of a bank deposit can be either positive or negative, which has important implications for hedging the interest-rate risk of bank balance sheets. Banks that maximize deposit value by following optimal deposit beta strategies may significantly increase their interest-rate and deposit runoff risks. We test the empirical implications of the valuation model using market deposit premia observed in bank merger/acquisition transactions. The results provide strong empirical support for the model’s predictions.

title: Ruling for the Rich: the Supreme Court over Time

detail.title: Ruling for the Rich: the Supreme Court over Time
detail.abstract:
To investigate the emergence of a pro-wealthy bias in the US Supreme Court, we develop a protocol to identify and analyze all cases involving economic issues from 1953 to the present. We categorize the parties in these cases as “rich” or “poor” according to their likelihood of being wealthy. A vote is pro-rich if that outcome would directly shift resources to the party that is more likely to be wealthy. Using this dataset, we estimate case-specific intercepts, justice-specific latent ideal points, and party-level time trends using the Bayesian methods pioneered by Martin and Quinn (2002). In the 1950s, justices appointed by the two parties appear similar in their propensity to cast pro-rich votes. Over the sample period, we estimate a steady increase in polarization, culminating in an implied party gap of 47 percentage points by 2022. The magnitude of the gap suggests the usefulness of an economic metric for prediction relative to ideologies such as originalism or textualism.

detail.title: Renewable Energy Expansion: Key Challenges and Emerging Opportunities
detail.abstract:
The global expansion of renewable energy is key to addressing climate change. After a decade of dramatic cost reductions—especially for solar photovoltaics and wind—renewables now approach cost parity with fossil generation. While this cost reduction has led to a steep increase in solar and wind power in several countries, the global share of solar and wind generation remains modest—approximately 15% as of 2023. This article reviews recent economic studies and identifies three central challenges and corresponding opportunities for scaling up renewable energy—underdeveloped regulatory and market design, insufficient intertemporal market integration, and inadequate spatial market integration. The insights from this review highlight effective ways to accelerate the global transition to renewable energy.

detail.title: Market Power and Capital Constraints
detail.abstract:
We explore how traders' equity capitalization influences asset prices in a framework that accounts for market power. In our model, traders with capital constraints engage in transactions in an imperfectly competitive market. We demonstrate that looser capital constraints elevate both asset prices and price impact, the latter diminishing market liquidity. Using Canadian Treasury auction data, we illustrate how to apply our model to quantify these effects. We estimate the shadow costs of capital constraints by leveraging a temporary policy exemption during 2020-2021. We show that while these constraints are only infrequently binding, their relative impact when activated can be sizable.

detail.title: Entry and Exit in Treasury Auctions
detail.abstract:
Hedge funds have become increasingly active in Treasury markets, yet we have little evidence on how this shift has affected the market. We focus on the primary market, where the government issues its debt through auctions. Using over 20 years of data from Canadian Treasury auctions, we document dealers exiting and hedge funds entering. To evaluate the costs and benefits of this trend for debt issuance, we develop an auction framework with endogenous participation. We find that the expected gains from greater hedge fund participation, driven by increased competition, are smaller than the costs that arise because hedge funds—unlike dealers—do not participate regularly. Currently, dealer participation remains sufficiently strong that policies aimed at stabilizing participation have little effect on funding costs.

title: The Morality Of Market Exchanges: Between Societal Values And Trade-Offs

detail.title: The Morality Of Market Exchanges: Between Societal Values And Trade-Offs
detail.abstract:
Onychomycosis is most commonly caused by dermatophytes, but non-dermatophytic fungi are increasingly recognized as relevant pathogens, especially in immunocompromised patients. We report a rare case of mixed onychomycosis caused by two non-dermatophytic molds. Cultures on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar revealed two distinct colonies, subsequently identified as Purpureocillium lilacinum by microscopic morphology and Fusarium solani by EUROArray Dermatomycosis assay and characteristic macroconidia. This co-infection highlights the pathogenic potential of non-dermatophytic fungi often considered contaminants. Both species exhibit poor susceptibility to conventional antifungals, complicating treatment. The case emphasizes the importance of integrated mycological and molecular diagnostics in atypical onychomycosis.

Certain behaviors in markets are unambiguously unethical. In other cases, however, voluntary exchanges that can create gains from trade remain contested on moral grounds, because of what is traded or of the price at which the exchange occurs. This chapter offers a framework to analyze these contested markets and provides examples of two general instances. First, we examine “repugnant” transactions involving the human body—such as compensated organ donation and gestational surrogacy—where concerns about dignity, exploitation, and inequality conflict with welfare gains from expanding supply. Second, we study price gouging in emergencies, where demands for a “just price” clash with the incentive and allocation roles of price adjustments under scarcity. Across both cases, we synthesize evidence on societal attitudes and highlight how support for policy options depends on perceived trade-offs between autonomy, fairness and efficiency, and on institutional features that can separate compensation from allocation.

title: Bayesian Inference in IV Regressions

detail.title: Bayesian Inference in IV Regressions
detail.abstract:
It is well known that standard frequentist inference breaks down in IV regressions with weak instruments. Bayesian inference with diffuse priors suffers from the same problem. We show that the issue arises because flat priors on the first-stage coefficients overstate instrument strength. In contrast, inference improves drastically when an uninformative prior is specified directly on the concentration parameter—the key nuisance parameter capturing instrument relevance. The resulting Bayesian credible intervals are asymptotically equivalent to the frequentist confidence intervals based on conditioning approaches, and remain robust to weak instruments.

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether a consistent, underlying pattern connects major economic crises, specifically, the decline of the real economy sector (agriculture and industry) alongside excessive financialization and service-sector expansion. Through a qualitative case study approach, we analyze historical GDP and sectoral data from four pivotal crises: the Great Depression, the European Debt Crisis, the Subprime Mortgage Crisis, and Sri Lanka's Economic Crisis. Our findings reveal a recurring structural vulnerability: each crisis was preceded by (1) declining productivity in the real sector, (2) a shift away from industrial and agricultural foundations, and (3) unsustainable growth in finance and services. These trends suggest that economic fragility arises not just from financial mismanagement but from deeper imbalances, where economies prioritize speculative and non-productive sectors over tangible value creation. This research contributes to crisis economics by proposing the Real Sector Neglect Hypothesis (RSNH), which reframes systemic collapses as structural, not only than purely cyclical or policy-driven, failures. The policy implication is clear: sustainable growth requires rebalancing toward productive sectors to enhance resilience against future shocks.

title: Self- and Social Signaling: Evidence from Solar Adoption in California

detail.title: Self- and Social Signaling: Evidence from Solar Adoption in California
detail.abstract:
Prosocial behavior plays a role in many economic contexts, and it has been explained by altruism, social pressure, signaling, and expectations of fairness and reciprocity. We examine prosocial behavior in a context that allows us to distinguish the role of self-signaling and social signaling from alternative explanations, including warm glow. Our context is residential solar, and self-signaling is separately identified from social signaling by the exogenous visibility of potential solar arrays. We show that the political affiliation of proximate peers influences the extent of self-signaling and is crowded out by the private benefits of installing solar.

detail.title: Green Waste
detail.abstract:
We test for and measure green waste: the misallocation of public subsidies for green investment projects. Our context is a major Norwegian program for green investment subsidies. We develop a model of subsidy allocation and apply it to detailed project-level data on carbon emissions and subsidy amounts for both marginal and inframarginal projects. We find that decision-makers could have achieved the same level of emission reductions at less than half the cost. To isolate the sources of this green waste, we use data on both ex-ante expected and ex-post realized emission reductions for each project. We find that decision-makers are able ex-ante to identify the projects with the highest ex-post emission reductions but unwilling to select them.

We show that commute time savings and improvements in employment accessibility are plausible mechanisms underlying these effects.

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion is widely recognized as a foundation for economic resilience and social stability. In the United States, a significant share of households remain unbanked or underbanked and continue to rely on cash, check-cashers, and high-cost alternative financial services for everyday transactions. This paper examines how payroll digitalization and employee banking platforms can support underbanked workers and contribute to financial inclusion in the U.S. context. Drawing on practices observed in Islamic and conventional banking markets, the paper argues that employer-linked payroll systems, supported by digital onboarding and Shariah-informed design principles, can create effective pathways into formal finance for low-income and vulnerable workers. The analysis is informed by international research and policy guidance from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the U.S. Treasury. The paper outlines the role of employee banking as a channel for inclusion, highlights the importance of digital tools such as tablet-based account opening and mobile banking, and explores how Islamic finance principles can enhance trust and consumer protection. It concludes with practical recommendations for U.S. financial institutions and policymakers seeking to expand access while maintaining strong standards of compliance and risk management.

title: The Bureaucratic Reliability Trap: Political Oversight and the Persistence of Corruption

detail.title: The Bureaucratic Reliability Trap: Political Oversight and the Persistence of Corruption
detail.abstract: Standard principal-agent models of corruption typically assume a benevolent principal monitoring a potential rogue agent. This paper relaxes that assumption to analyze bureaucratic reliability under dishonest political principals. Developing an infinite-horizon game of political oversight, I demonstrate that the shadow of the future acts as a double-edged sword: it resolves the commitment problem for honest principals to enforce reliability, but simultaneously empowers dishonest principals to enforce corruption via credible threats of permanent career derailment. Extending the analysis to endogenous rent-sharing, I find that standard anti-corruption parameters yield perverse outcomes under a dishonest principal: "cleaner" bureaucratic pools paradoxically strengthen the bargaining position of corrupt incumbents, while administrative penalties function as leverage for rent extraction rather than deterrence. Finally, the model characterizes a "Bureaucratic Reliability Trap" in which dishonest regimes induce path dependence by systematically purging public-minded agents, thereby entrenching corruption beyond the tenure of the original principal.

This study examines how digital incentives influence survey participation and engagement in a large randomized controlled trial of parents across seven Texas school districts. We test how incentive amount and information about vendor options affect response behavior and explore differences by language background. Incentivized parents were more likely to start and complete surveys and claim gift cards, though Spanish-speaking parents exhibited distinct patterns—greater completion rates but lower redemption rates, often selecting essential-goods vendors. Increasing incentive value and providing advance information both improved engagement. Findings inform the design of equitable, effective digital incentive strategies for diverse populations.

detail.title: Work from Home and the Narrative Reporting Quality
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of work-from-home (WFH) intensity on the narrative reporting quality. We use the city-level intensity of remote work job advertisements as a measure of exogenous pressure on firms to offer WFH opportunities to employees and find that firms headquartered in high-WFH pressure areas issue longer and more complex 10K filings. Occupational data analysis reveals that the effect is stronger when the share of remote work for financial specialists' positions increases, which suggests that the findings capture the difficulty in coordinating the preparation of financial statements among geographically distributed employees. Further tests indicate that the effect is not attributable to lower productivity among employees working from home, lower earnings quality, or declining financial performance. The effect is moderated when employees have more developed online social networks, and when employees are more likely to use AI for their tasks. Overall, the study identifies WFH intensity as a novel organizational determinant of disclosure quality.

title: Revaluing Consumer City: Amenity Usage and Housing Price Capitalization
affiliations: University College London

detail.title: Revaluing Consumer City: Amenity Usage and Housing Price Capitalization
detail.abstract: The Consumer City framework argues that urban growth is driven by access to diverse consumption opportunities rather than workplace proximity. Yet spatial proximity does not necessarily imply actual usage, especially in the work-from-home era, when mobility patterns have been fundamentally reshaped across urban space. We introduce the concept of the Amenity City, defined not by the presence of amenities but by their realized use. Drawing on 260 million anonymized mobile-phone records across England and Wales, we construct high-resolution measures of amenity-visit density at the 0.01 km² grid level in March 2020 and March 2021, and link them to 1.3 million repeat-sales housing transactions. Our analyses show that increases in amenity usage were rapidly capitalized into housing prices, with effects that became even stronger in the post-pandemic period. A spatial difference-indifferences design and event study analysis further reveals that neighborhoods with larger increases in amenity visits saw persistent appreciation in housing prices. We extend the Consumer City framework by demonstrating that not only proximity to amenities but also their actual use is capitalized into property values, providing implications for future research on human mobility and urban value.

title: Strategic Expression, Popularity Traps, and Welfare in Social Media
affiliations: University of Glasgow and Universite du Luxembourg - Luxembourg School of Finance

detail.title: Strategic Expression, Popularity Traps, and Welfare in Social Media
detail.abstract: Social media platforms systematically reward popularity but not authenticity, incentivizing users to strategically tailor their expression for attention. We develop a utilitarian framework addressing strategic expression in social media. Agents hold fixed heterogeneous authentic opinions and derive (i) utility gains from the popularity of their own posts-measured by likes received, and (ii) utility gains (losses) from exposure to content that aligns with (diverges from) their authentic opinion. Social media interaction acts as a state-dependent welfare amplifier: light topics generate Pareto improvements, whereas intense topics make everyone worse off in a polarized society (e.g., political debates during elections). Moreover, strategic expression amplifies social media polarization during polarized events while dampening it during unified events (e.g., national celebrations). Consequently, strategic distortions magnify welfare outcomes, expanding aggregate gains in light topics while exacerbating losses in intense, polarized ones. Counterintuitively, strategic agents often face a popularity trap: posting a more popular opinion is individually optimal, yet collective action by similar agents eliminates their authentic opinion from the platform, leaving them worse off than under the authentic-expression benchmark. Preference-based algorithms-widely used by platforms-or homophilic exposures discipline popularity-driven behavior, narrowing the popularity trap region and limiting its welfare effects. Our framework fills a critical gap in the social media literature by providing a microfoundation for user welfare that maps to observable metrics, while also introducing popularity incentives as an unexplored channel in social networks distinct from the canonical mechanisms of conformity, learning, persuasion, and (mis)information transmission.

Through a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative surveys of 187 financial organizations and qualitative interviews with 42 senior executives, this research identifies key determinants of implementation success. detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of unexpected changes in weather conditions on inflation in Korea. Using a structural vector autoregression (SVAR) model, we analyze how changes in temperature and precipitation influence price dynamics across different components of the consumer price index (CPI). Our empirical analysis reveals that unexpected changes in weather indices induce significant volatility in fresh food prices and exert direct impacts on consumer inflation, with precipitation changes contributing more substantially to short-term price increases than temperature variations. The effects are particularly pronounced during summer. However, core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, remains largely unresponsive to weather indices. Through a regression analysis examining the interaction between headline and core inflation, we find that consumer prices tend to revert to core inflation levels, suggesting that weather-induced price fluctuations have limited medium-term impacts on the underlying inflation trend. These findings indicate that while weather changes may increase short-term price volatility through agricultural supply disruptions, monetary policy responses to such temporary fluctuations may be ineffective. Accordingly, alternative policy measures focusing on supply diversification and climate resilience should be prioritized.

detail.title: Common Risk Premia for Stocks and Bonds
detail.abstract: We investigate risk-return trade-offs in stock and bond markets to develop a new equity market volatility factor of asset returns. Based on nonlinear regressions using equity-bond market volatilities of future returns, we document evidence for the shape of nonlinearity for risk-return trade-offs that supports the inverse reactions of stock and bond markets, known as flight-to-safety during periods of high equity market volatility. Using derivatives-implied volatility in equities over that in fixed income securities, we develop an excess volatility measure, termed VMV, that captures the nonlinear risk premia strongly. Our empirical analyses support that VMV is a significant predictor of asset returns during 2003 to 2019.

detail.title: Research Project Proposal: Bridging Keynes and Sraffa: the Z Function Grounded in Activatable Plants and Vertical Integration
detail.abstract: Starting from the Keynesian reading of D(N) and Z(N) as value magnitudes steered by expectations, we reconstruct Z(N) on classical-Sraffian foundations, avoiding the identification M P L = w/p. The key idea is to model aggregate supply as a piecewise linear frontier of branches/plants (vintages) evaluated at administered normal-cost prices, with slopes given by the value per unit of vertically integrated labour. This lets us treat capacity and technique changes as switches between segments without intra-period repricing, while preserving additivity of values. In the medium run, we re-benchmark to production prices consistent with distributive closure and the updated production structure; this rotates slopes and may generate reordering and reswitching. We show how the equilibrium condition D = Z determines the active segment j ⋆ , and we provide comparative statics (local, across periods, and global), including distributive implications for the wage share and the real wage. We extend the analysis to non-uniform rates/mark-ups, wage advances, and changes of numéraire; existence conditions remain governed by the spectral radius of A. The framework integrates Input-Output (Pasinetti-Leontief) accounting with the Keynesian employment determination, offering a theoretical and operational basis for empirical and policy analysis.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of environmental factors in enhancing the entrepreneurial effectiveness of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) engaged in fresh fruit sales in Bone-Bone Subdistrict, Baubau City. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed to explore the experiences of MSME actors, consumers, and key informants through participatory observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. The findings reveal that physical, social, economic, and technological environments significantly influence operational dynamics and business performance. Strategic location, proximity to supply centers, and strong social interactions support business stability, while challenges such as seasonal price fluctuations, limited capital, and low digital literacy hinder entrepreneurial effectiveness. Entrepreneurs who are able to interpret their environment, innovate, and adopt adaptive strategies demonstrate better performance, particularly through the use of social media, effective stock management, and strengthened social networks. Government involvement and community support also play crucial roles by providing training, assistance, and network facilitation. These findings underscore that the sustainability of fresh fruit MSMEs in Bone-Bone is shaped by the integration of internal entrepreneurial capacity with external environmental utilization. The study recommends strengthening multi-actor collaboration and enhancing digital literacy to improve competitiveness and ensure long-term MSME sustainability.

title: Restoring Convergence in Heavy-Tailed Risk Models: A Weighted Kolmogorov Approach for Robust Backtesting
